title: Aerolíneas Argentinas 707
summary: Aerolíneas Argentinas Flight 707, an Avro 748 with 37 occupants en route between Corrientes and Rosario, encountered severe turbulence while flying through a cumulonimbus cloud. The aircraft lost control, entered a steep left bank and dive, striking the ground. All 37 occupants perished.
probable_cause: loss of control of the airplane and collision with terrain when encountering a zone with adverse meteorological conditions and severe turbulence

the pilots lost control of the aircraft after it encountered severe turbulence, the plane entered a left bank of 90 degrees and entered a 45-degree dive

events.text: The aircraft flew into a cumulonimbus cloud while en route

title: Aeroflot U-45

location.name: mountainside 32 km northeast of Samarkand Airport

summary: Aeroflot Flight U-45, an Il-18 flying Tashkent-Samarkand in instrument meteorological conditions, was cleared to descend by approach control, but the controller misread the radar and reported the aircraft 31 km out when it was actually 42-44 km, prompting a premature descent before the mountain range was crossed. The crew, whose own radar was degraded by weather, missed a clue that the reported distances implied an impossible speed; at 14:42 the Il-18 struck a mountainside at 380 km/h, killing 92 of 106 aboard. The controller's misreading of the display scale was the primary cause, compounded by subpar ATC training.
probable_cause: The primary cause was the approach controller's misinterpretation of the radar display scale setting; contributing factors were subpar ATC training and a dark radar screen in high ambient light at Samarkand.

factors.evidence: The approach controller then misread his radar screen and reported the flight was 31 km out when in fact it was 42-44 km
a speed of approximately 1600 km/h would be needed... the crew missed this important clue and continued the descent
The organization and level of training of the ATC personnel at Samarkand International Airport was found to be subpar
the Il-18 crashed into the side of a mountain at a speed of 380 km/h while descending at seven meters per second

events.text: At 14:39 the approach controller advised the aircraft was 48 kilometers from the airport and cleared it to descend to 2,400 meters.
The controller then misread his radar screen and reported the flight was 31 km out when in fact it was 42 to 44 km, leading it to descend too early before crossing the mountain range.
The controller cleared the flight for landing on runway 09 and the crew accepted at 14:40, the last transmission from Flight U-45.
At 14:42, at 1,500 meters and 32 kilometers northeast of the airport, the Il-18 crashed into a mountainside at 380 km/h while descending at seven meters per second.

notes: Investigating agency not named in the text (pre-dates MAK).

title: Dominicana DC-9 air disaster
summary: Dominicana de Aviación Flight 603 crashed into the Caribbean Sea shortly after taking off from Santo Domingo for San Juan on 15 February 1970, killing all 97 passengers and five crew aboard. Two minutes after departure the right engine flamed out; while the crew were preparing to turn back, the left engine also flamed out, and the DC-9 descended into the sea about two miles south of the airport. The investigation concluded the sequential failure of both engines was caused by fuel contamination due to water ingress.
probable_cause: The cause of the crash was the sequential failure of both engines caused by fuel contamination due to water ingress.

factors.evidence: the cause of the crash was the sequential failure of both engines caused by fuel contamination due to water ingress
the right engine had flamed out... the left engine also flamed out
the aircraft descended until it hit the sea about two miles south of the airport

events.text: Two minutes after departure, the crew declared an emergency, telling air traffic controllers that the right engine had flamed out, and requested to return immediately to the airport.
While the crew were preparing to turn back toward the airport, the left engine also flamed out.
The aircraft descended until it hit the sea about two miles south of the airport; there were no survivors among the 97 passengers and five crew members aboard.

title: Swissair 330
summary: A bomb detonated in the cargo hold at approximately 12:15 UTC during southerly ascent over Lucerne north of the St. Gotthard Pass. The crew attempted to turn around for emergency landing at Zurich but had difficulty seeing instruments due to smoke in the cockpit. The aircraft deviated westward and crashed in a wooded area near Zurich due to loss of electrical power. All 47 passengers and crew were killed.
probable_cause: A barometric-triggered bomb detonated in the cargo hold, causing loss of electrical power and smoke in the cockpit that prevented the crew from maintaining control and returning to Zurich for emergency landing.

title: ALM 980
summary: A Douglas DC-9 operating for Overseas National Airways on behalf of ALM ditched in the Caribbean Sea on 2 May 1970 after fuel exhaustion following three unsuccessful landing attempts and diversions. The crew miscalculated fuel consumption, misread fuel gauges, and incorrectly computed fuel reserves, compounding high workload from weather and multiple approach attempts. The aircraft ditched 48 kilometers off St. Croix with 23 fatalities, though the crew successfully coordinated evacuation through open cargo doors despite initially poor coordination.
probable_cause: Poor fuel management resulting from miscalculation of fuel consumption rate, misreading of fuel gauges, and incorrect computation of fuel quantity, complicated by crew inattention and distraction from weather conditions and multiple landing attempts.

factors.evidence: The crew miscalculated the rate of fuel consumption, misread fuel gauges, and incorrectly computed the amount of fuel expected to remain.

Crew inattention and distraction resulted in poor fuel management throughout the descent and approach phase.
The aircraft's fuel was exhausted and the captain advised ATC of his intention to ditch the aircraft.
Flight 980 ditched in the Caribbean Sea at 3:49 pm local time.

title: Dan-Air 1903

location.name: Les Agudes, Serralada del Montseny, near Arbúcies

summary: Dan-Air Flight 1903 crashed into the Serralada del Montseny near Arbúcies during a descent toward Barcelona on 3 July 1970, killing all 112 aboard the Comet 4. The crew mistakenly reported passing the Sabadell NDB while still 28 nmi north of it over mountainous terrain; the controller, misled by a radar echo from another aircraft over Sabadell, did not notice the error and cleared the crew to keep descending to 2800 ft. The aircraft struck beech trees on the Les Agudes peak at about 3800 ft.
probable_cause: An involuntary mutual error between crew and ATC: erroneous position reporting by the crew combined with a radar echo from another aircraft near Sabadell led the controller to believe the Comet had passed the beacon, and this could not be corrected before the aircraft struck high terrain.

factors.evidence: they were still 28 nmi north of Sabadell at the time, over the Serralada del Montseny

Barcelona ATC mistook that second aircraft's radar echo for that of the Dan-Air Comet
the aircraft crashed into a group of beech trees on the northeast slopes of the Les Agudes peak at an altitude of about 3800 ft

events.text: Flight 1903 departed Manchester Airport at 16:08 BST and encountered air traffic control delays in the Paris area, resulting in a change of route.
Radio contact was established with Barcelona Area Control Centre at 17:53 local time, and the crew was cleared to descend from Flight Level 220 to FL090.
Six minutes later the flight was handed to Barcelona approach control, which cleared the crew to overfly the Sabadell NDB and descend further to FL060.
While carrying out the turn, the crew reported in error that they had passed the Sabadell NDB, though they were still 28 nautical miles north of it, over the Serralada del Montseny.
Barcelona ATC mistook the radar echo of another aircraft overflying Sabadell for the Dan-Air Comet and cleared the crew to continue descending to 2800 ft.
At about 19:05 CEST the Comet struck a group of beech trees on the northeast slopes of the Les Agudes peak at an altitude of about 3800 ft and was destroyed in the explosion.

notes: Agency AAIB inferred from the UK AAIB report link; not explicitly named in the article text.

title: Air Canada 621
summary: Air Canada Flight 621, a Douglas DC-8 landing at Toronto on 5 July 1970, touched down hard which ruptured the right fuel tanks. The investigation attributed the accident to pilot error and non-compliance with spoiler deployment procedures, where the first officer deployed spoilers during the flare instead of arming them.
probable_cause: The crew deviated from approved spoiler procedures; the first officer deployed spoilers during the flare instead of arming them, causing the aircraft to sink heavily and resulting in a hard landing that ruptured fuel tanks which subsequently exploded.

factors.evidence: The first officer immediately deployed the spoilers on the flare instead of just arming them
The aircraft began to sink heavily and the captain pulled back on the control column and applied full thrust, the aircraft still continued to sink
the right wing's fuel tanks exploded thrice
the aircraft crashed in Toronto Gore Township

events.text: Sixty feet from the runway, the captain began to reduce power in preparation for the flare.
The first officer immediately deployed the spoilers on the flare instead of just arming them.
The aircraft began to sink heavily after the spoilers were deployed during the flare.
The captain pulled back on the control column and applied full thrust to all four engines.
During landing at Toronto, the aircraft touched down hard, which ruptured the right fuel tanks.
After a go-around, the right wing's fuel tanks exploded thrice during flight.
The aircraft crashed in Toronto Gore Township, now part of Brampton.

title: LANSA 502
summary: Four-engine Electra turboprop lost number three engine power and fire immediately after takeoff at 10,860 feet elevation airport. Crew properly continued takeoff on three remaining engines per standard procedure. During emergency return to runway crew incorrectly retracted flaps while attempting approach. Aircraft entered steep 30 to 45 degree bank and rapidly descended into mountainous terrain 1.5 miles from runway. Post-crash fire consumed fuel and killed all aboard except copilot. Investigation concluded improper crew execution of engine-out procedures and inadequate maintenance by operator caused the crash.
probable_cause: Failure of number three engine immediately after takeoff, followed by crew failure to properly execute engine-out procedures and retraction of flaps, resulting in loss of control and terrain impact.

factors.evidence: number three engine failed and caught fire during the takeoff run
the crew incorrectly retracted the flaps and maneuvered the plane into a left turn back to the runway

events.text: At about 2:55 pm during the takeoff run the number three engine failed and caught fire.
The crew continued the takeoff and climb, per standard procedure, using power from the remaining three engines.
The pilot radioed the control tower declaring an emergency, and the control tower cleared the flight for an immediate landing.
The number three engine was engulfed in flames as the crew incorrectly retracted the flaps and maneuvered the plane into a left turn back to the runway.
The plane entered a 30 to 45 degree bank, then rapidly lost altitude and crashed into hilly terrain about 1.5 miles west-southwest of the runway above the village of San Jerónimo.
The fuel on board caught fire and all aboard perished except the copilot.

title: Southern Airways 932
summary: Southern Airways Flight 932, a DC-9-30 chartered by Marshall University, crashed into a hill 5,543 feet short of Tri-State Airport on 14 November 1970, killing all 75 occupants including 37 football players, 5 coaches, and 2 pilots. The crew descended below minimum descent altitude during approach without visual contact in rain, fog, and smoke. An altimetry system error or improper instrument use led to the controlled flight into terrain.
probable_cause: Descent below Minimum Descent Altitude during a nonprecision approach under adverse operating conditions without visual contact with the runway environment; probable explanations include improper use of cockpit instrumentation data or altimetry system error.

factors.evidence: The aircraft did not arrest its descent and hold altitude at 1240 feet as required by the assigned instrument approach procedure, and instead descended another 300 feet.
The co-pilot called out altitudes but pilots continued descent below minimums without recognizing the violation.
Air traffic control advised that rain, fog, smoke and a ragged ceiling were at the airport, making landing more difficult.

The aircraft approached the Catlettsburg Refinery in the final 30 seconds before impact, which could have affected a visual illusion produced by the difference in elevation of the refinery and airport.
The aircraft collided with the tops of trees on a hillside and crashed in a nose-first attitude.

events.text: Flight 932 crew established radio contact with air traffic control with instructions to descend to 5000 feet.
Controller advised crew that rain, fog, smoke and a ragged ceiling were at the airport.
Aircraft began normal descent after passing the outer marker but did not arrest descent as required by instrument approach procedure.
Co-pilot called out altitude readings: 'seven hundred feet...We're two hundred above [approach minimums]' and then 'four hundred'.
Aircraft descended another 220 feet within 12 seconds and collided with tree tops on a hillside 5543 feet short of runway, burst into flames.
